# Model Evaluation {#sec-results}

Having developed the theory of GPs and DGPs and derived the variational inference framework needed for scalable training, this section evaluates DGP models empirically. We compare GPs and DGPs against standard machine learning baselines across two datasets.

The first experiment uses the Kin8nm robot kinematics dataset (@sec-kin8nm), a regression benchmark with known non-stationary, compositional structure where we expect DGPs to outperform single-layer GPs. This establishes whether the additional depth of DGPs translates into measurable gains when the data likely supports it.

The second experiment applies the same model families to financial credit-risk classification, specifically probability of default on the UCI credit card dataset (@sec-credit-card). This tests if DGPs add any meaningful value on real-world financial data, while also evaluating GPs/DGPs native probability calibration, which is directly important under finance regulations such as Basel IRB [@basel_committee_basel_2011]. The aim is to see if the additional flexibility of DGPs gives a meaningful performance boost on a real financial data task, or simply incurs additional computational cost without improving performance over single-layer GPs.

Across both experiments, the model set comprises three classical baselines (linear model, random forest, XGBoost) and three GP-family models (SVGP, DSVGP-2L, DSVGP-3L). Each experiment evaluates performance at multiple training-set sizes to characterise scaling behaviour.

### Evaluation Metrics

Regression performance is measured by RMSE, R², and negative log predictive density (NLPD). NLPD evaluates the full predictive distribution: for test observations $\{(\vx_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n_*}$ it is

$$
\text{NLPD} = -\frac{1}{n_*} \sum_{i=1}^{n_*} \log p(y_i \mid \vx_i, \mathcal{D}),
$$ {#eq-nlpd}

where $y_i$ is the observed (noisy) output. For GP models with a Gaussian predictive distribution $\mathcal{N}(y_i \mid \mu_i, \sigma_i^2)$, this reduces to $\frac{1}{n_*}\sum_i \bigl[\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma_i^2) + \frac{(y_i - \mu_i)^2}{2\sigma_i^2}\bigr]$, where $\sigma_i^2$ includes observation noise $\sigma_n^2$. Lower NLPD is better. Unlike RMSE, NLPD penalises both inaccurate means and poorly calibrated predictive variance, which makes it one of the primary metric for assessing uncertainty quality. Classical models (Ridge, Random Forest, XGBoost) do not produce predictive distributions, so NLPD is reported only for GP-family models.

Classification performance is measured by ROC-AUC, average precision, F1 at the validation-chosen threshold $t^*$, expected calibration error (ECE), Brier score, and log loss. ECE measures calibration by binning predictions and comparing average predicted probability to observed frequency within each bin; lower ECE indicates better-calibrated probability estimates.

Hyperparameters for all models were fixed based on established defaults from prior work rather than tuned via search. For classical baselines, logistic/ridge regression uses default regularisation ($C=1$), random forest uses 500 trees with balanced class weighting, and XGBoost uses learning rate 0.05 with early stopping on the validation set to select the number of boosting rounds. For GP-family models, SVGP uses 512 inducing points trained for 150 epochs, and DSVGP models use 128 inducing points per layer with hidden dimension 5. These were chosen as practical defaults for the dataset scales based on available compute resources and converging in a reasonable time frame. All GP/DGP kernel hyperparameters (lengthscales, output variance, noise variance) are learnt jointly with the variational parameters by maximising the ELBO during training.
